templates.title: Consumer groups whose lag keeps growing
templates.subtopic: carry-forward lookups, LAG and gaps-and-islands streaks

sections.scenario: A streaming platform team watches consumer lag. For a consumer group and a partition, offset lag is how far the group's last committed offset is behind the partition's log-end offset (the offset the next record will receive), which is how public documentation describes it. One high reading is normal after a deploy or a rebalance; lag that rises at snapshot after snapshot means the group is not keeping up and someone should look. A collector snapshots log-end offsets and committed offsets every {{interval}}. You have {{snapshots}} snapshots covering {{groups}} groups, and the team wants every stretch where a group's total lag kept growing.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns group_id, streak_start, streak_end, increases, lag_at_start, lag_at_end. A partition's lag at a snapshot is log_end_offset − committed_offset, and a group's total lag at a snapshot is the sum of the lags of every partition it consumes, across topics. {{clamp_rule}} {{rows_rule}} A streak is a maximal run of consecutive snapshots of one group in which each snapshot's total lag is strictly greater than the previous snapshot's. Report every streak with at least {{streak}} increases: streak_start is the taken_at of the snapshot just before the first increase (the baseline), streak_end the taken_at of the last increase, increases the number of increases, and lag_at_start and lag_at_end the group's total lag at those two snapshots. Order by group_id, streak_start.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Snapshot ids increase with time but are not consecutive; order snapshots by taken_at. Every snapshot has a log_end_offsets row for every partition of every topic.
sections.assumptions: Groups, topics, offsets, the snapshot interval and the collector are hypothetical. Lag here is measured in records (offsets), not in time; a consumer that commits rarely looks laggier than it is, which is acceptable for this report.
sections.criteria: Total lag per group per snapshot over every consumed partition, across topics; snapshots ordered by time, not by id arithmetic; strictly greater comparison; streaks counted in increases with the baseline snapshot as the start; negative partition lag clamped to 0 before summing (Hard+); the latest committed offset carried forward and partitions counted from their first commit (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss time-based lag, streaming detection and offset resets.

clarifications.q: Does an equal total continue a streak?
clarifications.a: No. An equal or lower total ends the streak; the next increase starts a new one.

clarifications.q: Is streak_start the first snapshot that grew?
clarifications.a: No, it is the snapshot just before it, the baseline the growth is measured from. A streak of N increases spans N + 1 snapshots.

clarifications.q: Can I find the previous snapshot with snapshot_id − 1?
clarifications.a: No. Ids have gaps; order by taken_at.

clarifications.q: A group consumes two topics. Is that one total or two?
clarifications.a: One total per group, over every partition it consumes in both topics.

clarifications.q: Can a group have two separate streaks?
clarifications.a: Yes. Report each one that has enough increases.

hints: Build one row per (group, snapshot) with its total lag first. The streak logic is much easier on that small table.
LAG(total_lag) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY taken_at) gives the previous total; mark each row as an increase or not.
Number the islands with a running SUM of "not an increase" flags: the increases of one streak share a number. Within a streak the totals only rise, so MIN and MAX give the start and end lag.
If a partition can be missing at a snapshot, its committed offset is the latest row at or before that snapshot: a correlated subquery with ORDER BY taken_at DESC LIMIT 1, or a LATERAL join.
followups: Offset lag counts records. How would you report lag in time (the age of the oldest unconsumed record), and what extra data would the collector need?
Thousands of groups are snapshotted every minute. How would you detect these streaks continuously, as each snapshot arrives, instead of with a batch query?
During a planned backfill, lag grows on purpose for hours. How would you keep this alert from firing without hiding a real stall in the same group?
A group's committed offsets are reset to the latest offset and its lag drops to zero, skipping records. How would this report hide that, and what would you add to catch it?

rules.ask: Snapshot ids have gaps. What does a join on snapshot_id − 1 return right after a gap, and how else can you find the previous snapshot?
Two snapshots in a row have the same total lag. Does your comparison continue the streak, and should it?
How do you turn ROW_NUMBER into island ids here, and what has to be true about the rows you number for the difference trick to work?
At a snapshot where a partition has no committed-offset row, what does your join do to that group's total, and is the group really caught up there?
Why clamp each partition's lag at zero before summing, rather than clamping the group's total?

templates.title: Hot partitions: topic-hours where one partition takes far more than its share
templates.subtopic: two-level aggregation, top-1 per group, as-of lookups, exact ratio comparisons

sections.scenario: Producers choose a partition by hashing the record key, so a few very busy keys can send far more traffic to one partition than to the others. A hot partition overloads the broker that leads it and caps how fast its consumers can go, however many consumers the group has. The platform team samples bytes received per partition every 20 minutes and wants every topic-hour where the busiest partition took more than {{k}} times the topic's mean, as long as the topic carried at least {{min_mb}} MB that hour (skew on a nearly idle topic is noise).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns topic, hour_start, busiest_partition, busiest_bytes, mean_bytes, skew_ratio. For each topic and UTC hour (date_trunc('hour', sample_ts)), sum bytes_in per partition. The mean is the topic-hour's total bytes divided by the topic's partition count, busiest_bytes is the largest per-partition total (ties go to the lower partition_id), and skew_ratio = busiest_bytes / mean. Report a topic-hour when its total is at least {{min_bytes}} bytes and busiest_bytes is strictly greater than {{k}} times the mean. Round mean_bytes to 2 decimal places and skew_ratio to 3. Order by topic, hour_start. {{idle_rule}} {{count_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{samples}} rows. The partition count comes from partition_count_changes, never from the partitions that happen to have rows. Compare exactly: a ratio exactly {{k}} is not reported.
sections.assumptions: Topics, partition counts, byte volumes, the thresholds and the sampling interval are hypothetical. Bytes in is measured at the partition leader; replication traffic is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Two-level aggregation with per-partition hourly totals; the mean divides by the topic's partition count, including idle partitions (Hard+), as of the end of the hour when partitions are added (Very Hard); duplicates removed (Very Hard); busiest partition with the lower-id tie-break; inclusive floor and strict exact ratio comparison; correct rounding; UTC hours; deterministic order; can explain hot keys, repartitioning trade-offs and how to run this at scale.

clarifications.q: Is the mean over the partitions that had traffic?
clarifications.a: No, over all of the topic's partitions. An idle partition is part of the imbalance.

clarifications.q: Is the floor inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes: a topic-hour with total exactly {{min_bytes}} bytes qualifies.

clarifications.q: Which hour does a sample belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC hour of sample_ts; each sample covers the 20 minutes after it.

clarifications.q: Two partitions tie for busiest. Which one do I report?
clarifications.a: The lower partition_id.

clarifications.q: Should I compare the rounded ratio with the threshold?
clarifications.a: No. Compare exact values; rounding is only for display.

hints: Aggregate twice: samples to (topic, hour, partition), then partitions to (topic, hour).
DISTINCT ON (topic, hour_start) … ORDER BY topic, hour_start, bytes DESC, partition_id picks the busiest partition with the tie-break.
busiest > k × total / count is the same as busiest × count > k × total, which avoids division entirely.
If the count can change, look it up as of the hour: the latest partition_count_changes row whose effective_at is before the right moment.
followups: You find a hot partition. How would you tell whether it comes from one heavy key, many keys that hash together, or a producer that does not spread records across partitions?
The fix proposed is to add partitions. What happens to the ordering of records for existing keys, and to consumers of a compacted topic?
Bytes in is one signal. What other per-partition measures (messages, consumer lag, leader placement) would make the report more useful, and how would you combine them?
At thousands of topics with per-partition metrics every 10 seconds, how would you compute this continuously and keep a year of it cheaply?

rules.ask: Is your mean an average over partitions or over sample rows? How many partitions does an hour with an idle partition have in your query?
If you count the partitions that appear in the samples, what happens in an hour where one partition received nothing at all?
Two partitions tie for busiest. How many rows does your query return for that topic-hour?
Do you round before or after comparing with the threshold? Show a value where the order changes the answer.
After adding partitions, where do existing keys go, and what does that do to per-key ordering?

templates.title: Under-replicated minutes and time below min in-sync replicas
templates.subtopic: state intervals from change events, clipping to a window, interval union

sections.scenario: Each partition has a replication factor (how many brokers hold a copy) and an in-sync replica set (ISR): the replicas that are caught up with the leader. A partition whose ISR is smaller than its replication factor is under-replicated: it still works but has less redundancy. If the ISR falls below the topic's min.insync.replicas, producers that wait for all in-sync replicas (acks=all) have their writes rejected, so for them the topic is partly unavailable. The team logs every ISR size change and wants a daily report for the UTC day {{day}}.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over the window [{{window_start}}, {{window_end}}) that returns topic, under_replicated_partitions, urp_partition_minutes, below_min_isr_minutes. Each isr_changes row gives a partition's ISR size from changed_at until that partition's next change. For each topic: under_replicated_partitions is the number of its partitions that spent any time in the window with isr_size < replication_factor; urp_partition_minutes is that time summed over its partitions; and below_min_isr_minutes is the time during which at least one of its partitions had isr_size < min_insync_replicas (overlapping partitions count once). Minutes are seconds / 60, rounded to 2 decimal places. Return only topics with some under-replicated time, ordered by topic. {{start_rule}} {{settings_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The sample has {{changes}} change rows. Clip every interval to the window. No partition has two changes at the same second.
sections.assumptions: Topics, replication settings and ISR changes are hypothetical. ISR size is enough here; which replicas were in the set is out of scope. Below-min time is a proxy for "some acks=all writes would fail", whether or not anyone was writing.
sections.criteria: Intervals from change rows with LEAD computed over all rows; the state at the window start carried in (Hard+); clipping at both window edges, including a change exactly at the end; strict comparisons with the replication factor and the minimum; distinct partition counts; below-min time as a union of intervals per topic, merged against the running maximum end (Very Hard has a nested interval); per-topic settings; correct rounding; can discuss attributing failures, settings history, alerting and broker attribution.

clarifications.q: Is a partition with ISR exactly min_insync_replicas below the minimum?
clarifications.a: No. At exactly the minimum, acks=all writes still succeed; only fewer is below.

clarifications.q: Two partitions are below the minimum at the same time. Does that count twice?
clarifications.a: Not in below_min_isr_minutes: it is the time the topic had at least one partition below. In urp_partition_minutes each partition's time counts.

clarifications.q: Where does a partition's state at the window start come from?
clarifications.a: From its latest change at or before the window start.

clarifications.q: A partition's last change is in the afternoon. How long does that state last?
clarifications.a: Until the window end, unless the partition changes again first.

clarifications.q: What about a change exactly at {{window_end}}?
clarifications.a: It belongs to the next day and adds nothing here.

hints: Turn change rows into intervals with LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY topic, partition_id ORDER BY changed_at), before filtering to the window, so the interval in force at the window start is kept.
Clip with GREATEST(start, window_start) and LEAST(COALESCE(next, window_end), window_end), then keep intervals with end > start.
The topic-level below-min time is the length of a union of intervals: sort by start, start a new island when an interval begins after the largest end seen so far, and add up the islands.
"The largest end so far" is MAX(e) OVER (… ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING); the previous row's end alone is not enough.
followups: The report says a topic spent 40 minutes below the minimum. How would you tell which producers actually had writes rejected, and what data would you need?
Replication factor and min.insync.replicas can change during the day. How would you model their history and use it here?
How would you turn this into an alert that fires when a partition has been under-replicated for more than ten minutes, without paging on every short ISR shrink during a rolling restart?
Across a large fleet, under-replicated partitions often share one broker. How would you attribute the minutes to brokers, and what extra data does that need?

rules.ask: Do you compute LEAD before or after filtering to the window? Which row gives a partition's state at the window start in each case?
Three intervals: [1:00, 3:00), [1:10, 1:20) and [2:00, 4:00). If you compare each start with the previous row's end, what total do you get, and what is right?
Two partitions of the same topic are below the minimum at the same time. Does your below-min total count those minutes once or twice?
A partition has exactly min_insync_replicas in sync. Can an acks=all producer still write to it?
You expand the day into minutes. What happens to a change at 10:00:30, and how big does this get for a month of a large cluster?

templates.title: What a log-compaction pass leaves behind
templates.subtopic: last occurrence per key in one pass, with range and time rules

sections.scenario: A compacted topic keeps at least the latest record for each key instead of deleting by age, which makes it a durable changelog of current state (account settings, customer profiles). A record with a null value is a tombstone: it marks the key as deleted and is itself removed some time later, so consumers that read from the beginning still have a chance to see the delete. The team wants to predict exactly which offsets a compaction pass will leave, to check a restored replica and to explain to a consumer why an old offset is gone. The rules below are this exercise's simplified model of compaction; check current docs for the product's actual behaviour.
sections.problem:
Implement compact(records, active_start, now_ms, delete_retention_ms, min_lag_ms). Each record is (partition, offset, key, value, ts_ms); value is None for a tombstone. Within each partition, records are listed in offset order (partitions may be interleaved). active_start[p] is the base offset of partition p's active segment, which is never compacted. Per partition:

  1. The cleanable range is every record with offset below active_start[p]. {{lag_rule}}
  2. A record in the cleanable range is removed if a later record (higher offset) with the same key is also in the cleanable range. Records outside the range never remove anything.
  3. A tombstone in the cleanable range that is not removed by rule 2 is still dropped when ts_ms <= now_ms - delete_retention_ms (its delete horizon has passed).
  4. Every other record stays, including every record outside the cleanable range.

Return {partition: [offsets that remain, ascending]} with an entry for every partition in active_start. {{parts_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 records and 60 000 distinct keys. Expected: O(n) time with a dict. Rescanning the log for each key or for each record is O(n × keys) and too slow.
sections.assumptions: Keys, values, timestamps and settings are hypothetical. Offsets are never renumbered by compaction, which is why a consumer can see gaps. Real compaction works segment by segment and decides tombstone removal differently; this model keeps only the parts needed for the exercise.
sections.criteria: Partitions handled independently; the cleanable range ends at the active segment (and at the first too-young record in Very Hard, even when later records look older); one pass that records each key's last offset inside the range; records outside the range kept and never used to supersede; the tombstone horizon applied with <= only to surviving tombstones; offsets returned ascending with an entry for every partition, including empty ones; O(n); can explain memory limits, tombstone retention and what consumers observe.

clarifications.q: A key's newest record is in the active segment. Does it remove the key's older records?
clarifications.a: No. Only records inside the cleanable range count when deciding what is superseded, so the older record stays until a later pass.

clarifications.q: Is a tombstone exactly at the horizon kept?
clarifications.a: No. ts_ms <= now_ms - delete_retention_ms is dropped; one millisecond newer is kept.

clarifications.q: A key is deleted with a tombstone and then written again. What remains?
clarifications.a: If the new value is in the cleanable range, it supersedes the old value and the tombstone, so only it remains.

clarifications.q: Do keys interact across partitions?
clarifications.a: No. Each partition is compacted on its own.

clarifications.q: Can I sort the records?
clarifications.a: You may, but they are already in offset order within each partition, and a single pass is enough.

hints: Group records by partition first; everything after that is per partition.
Find where the cleanable range ends, then make one pass that stores each key's last offset inside it.
A record in the range survives only if it is its key's last offset; then apply the tombstone horizon to the survivors.
Keep the comparisons exact: > for "too young to clean", <= for "past the horizon".
followups: The offset map for 60 000 keys fits in memory. What changes when a partition has a billion distinct keys, and how could you bound the memory a pass needs?
A consumer reads the topic from the beginning but is slow, so it starts after a tombstone was dropped. What does it see for that key, and how should delete_retention_ms be chosen?
Compaction runs segment by segment, in the background. Which records can a consumer see that this model says are gone, and does that break any guarantee?
Why does a compacted topic still need a minimum compaction lag for some consumers, and what does it cost in disk?

rules.ask: How many times does your code scan the log, and how long will that take for 60 000 keys and 300 000 records?
The records are already in offset order per partition. What does sorting cost you, and do you need it at all?
A key's newest record is in the active segment. Which of its older records survive this pass, and why?
A tombstone is the last record for its key and is exactly at the delete horizon. Is it kept, and what does a consumer that starts reading later miss?
Which part of this problem needs ordering at all, and could a plain dict do it?

templates.title: Which log segments retention deletes
templates.subtopic: prefix deletion under time, size and offset limits

sections.scenario: A partition's log is stored as a sequence of segment files; the newest is the active segment, still being written. Retention deletes whole segments from the oldest end, by age (retention.ms) and by size (retention.bytes, per partition), and a delete-records request can move the log start offset forward. Before a disk-capacity change, the team wants to predict, per partition, how many segments and bytes the next retention check frees and where each log will start afterwards. The rules below are this exercise's simplified model; check current docs for the product's actual behaviour.
sections.problem:
Implement apply_retention(partitions, configs, now_ms). Each partition is (topic, partition_id, log_start_offset, segments); segments is a list of (base_offset, size_bytes, max_ts_ms), oldest first, and the last one is the active segment. configs[topic] = (retention_ms, retention_bytes), where -1 means no limit. For each partition, in this order, never deleting the active segment:

  1. Time: from the oldest, delete each segment with now_ms − max_ts_ms > retention_ms; stop at the first segment that does not qualify.
  2. Size: let total be the size of all remaining segments, the active one included. From the oldest remaining, delete a segment while total − its size >= retention_bytes, subtracting it from total; stop at the first that does not qualify.
  3. Log start: {{start_rule}}

Return {(topic, partition_id): (deleted_segments, deleted_bytes, new_log_start_offset)}. {{limits_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 80 partitions with 10 000 segments each. Every partition has at least one segment. Expected: O(s) per partition with one running total. Recomputing the remaining size after every deletion is O(s²) and too slow.
sections.assumptions: Segment sizes, timestamps, limits and the request are hypothetical. max_ts_ms is the largest record timestamp in the segment. A real broker may roll the active segment so that it can be deleted, and it schedules deletions asynchronously; neither is modelled.
sections.criteria: Time, then size, then log start, in that order; the active segment never deleted but counted in the size total; strict > for age and inclusive >= for size; time deletion stops at the first unexpired segment; -1 handled as no limit for each limit (Hard+); the log-start rule by the next segment's base offset, with the new start the larger of the request and the first remaining base (Very Hard); one running total, O(s); can discuss timestamp skew, tiered storage and capacity forecasting.

clarifications.q: Does the active segment count toward total?
clarifications.a: Yes. It holds bytes on disk; it just cannot be deleted.

clarifications.q: Is a segment exactly retention_ms old deleted?
clarifications.a: No. It must be strictly older: now_ms − max_ts_ms > retention_ms.

clarifications.q: After deleting a segment, can the rest be exactly retention_bytes?
clarifications.a: Yes. Deletion continues while what is left would still be at least retention_bytes.

clarifications.q: A segment further back has expired but an older one has not. Is it deleted by time?
clarifications.a: No. Time deletion stops at the first segment that has not expired; size retention may still remove it.

clarifications.q: Do the limits apply to the topic as a whole?
clarifications.a: No, to each partition separately.

hints: Deletion only ever removes a prefix of the segment list, so keep one index of the first remaining segment.
Compute the remaining size once after the time step, then subtract as you delete.
The log-start step compares the next segment's base offset, because a segment is wholly below the log start offset only when the following segment begins at or before it.
followups: Producers set record timestamps, and one sends timestamps a week in the future. What does that do to time retention, and how would you protect against it?
A topic keeps 30 days but its consumers only read the last hour. With tiered storage, how would you split retention between local disk and object storage, and what changes in this calculation?
How would you use this function to forecast disk usage a week ahead per broker, given producer byte rates per partition?
The size limit is per partition. A topic doubles its partition count. What happens to its total disk use, and how would you explain that to its owner?

rules.ask: How many times does your code add up a partition's segment sizes? What does that cost for 10 000 segments with 7 500 deleted?
What does removing from the front of a Python list cost, and how can you avoid moving any data at all?
A segment in the middle carries a timestamp from the future. Which segments does time retention delete, and which does size retention delete?
Does your total include the active segment? What would change if it did not?
The log start offset is in the middle of a segment. Is that segment deleted, and what is the new log start offset?

templates.title: Sticky rebalance — a balanced assignment that moves the fewest partitions
templates.subtopic: heaps, balanced assignment with minimal movement

sections.scenario: The {{group}} consumer group reads several topics, and each partition must be consumed by exactly one member of the group. When members join or leave, the group rebalances and an assignor decides who owns what. Every partition that changes owner costs something: the old owner stops, the new owner rebuilds local state and caches, and processing on that partition pauses while it moves. A sticky assignor therefore keeps the assignment balanced while moving as few partitions as possible. You are writing the assignment step.
sections.problem:
Implement rebalance(partitions, members, owned). partitions lists every (topic, partition) the group subscribes to now, in any order. members lists the member ids in the group now. owned lists the last known ownership as (member, generation, [(topic, partition), ...]), one row per member; it can include members that have since left. Return a dict that maps every member in members to its sorted list of partitions. Partitions sort by topic, then by partition number. Member ids compare as strings. Apply these rules, which are this exercise's rules (real assignors differ in detail; check the client documentation):

  1. Valid claims. A claim counts only if its member is still in the group and its partition still exists. If several members claim one partition, the claim with the highest generation wins. If two or more members share that highest generation, nobody keeps the partition. A member's valid claims are its retained partitions.
  2. Quotas. With P partitions and C members, every member gets ⌊P/C⌋ partitions, and P mod C members get one more. The extra places go to the members with the most retained partitions, and ties go to the smaller member id.
  3. Keep. Each member keeps its lowest retained partitions, up to its quota, and releases the rest.
  4. Place. Every partition nobody kept is free. Free partitions are taken in ascending order. Each one goes to the member that holds the fewest partitions at that moment, among members still below their quota. Ties go to the smaller member id.

If members is empty, return {}. {{replay_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 partitions and 5 000 members. Up to 150 000 partitions can be free in one rebalance. Something close to O(P log P + P log C) is expected. Scanning every member for every free partition is O(P·C) and is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Group sizes, topics and generations are hypothetical. Every member subscribes to every topic in partitions. A partition appears at most once in partitions and at most once in one member's list. Each member appears at most once in owned.
sections.criteria: Valid claims only (members still in the group, partitions that still exist, highest generation, ties left unowned); quotas that give the extra places to the members retaining the most, with the id tie-break; overloaded members release their highest partitions; free partitions placed in ascending order to the least-loaded member with room; numeric partition order; {} for an empty group; a heap or another O(log C) placement; a clear argument that the result is balanced and moves the fewest partitions; sensible answers on cooperative rebalancing and weighted load.

clarifications.q: Does the result have to move the fewest partitions?
clarifications.a: Yes, and these rules guarantee it. Giving the extra places to the members that retain the most, and keeping up to the quota, keeps as many partitions as any balanced assignment can. The rules also fix which of the many optimal answers you return.

clarifications.q: Which retained partitions does an overloaded member release?
clarifications.a: Its highest ones. It keeps the lowest, up to its quota.

clarifications.q: Does ('orders', 10) sort before ('orders', 2)?
clarifications.a: No. The partition number is an integer, so 2 comes before 10.

clarifications.q: What happens to claims from a member that left?
clarifications.a: They are ignored, and those partitions are free.

clarifications.q: Can there be more members than partitions?
clarifications.a: Yes. Then the quota is 0 or 1, and some members get an empty list.

hints: Work out the quota of every member before you place anything. Once quotas are fixed, every free partition just needs a member with room.

"The member with the fewest partitions, then the smallest id" is the minimum of the key (count, member). A heap of members below quota gives that in O(log C), and a member goes back in only while it still has room.
Resolve claims in one pass over owned, keeping the best (generation, member) per partition and marking a tie at the top generation.
followups: Your function runs for the whole group in one place. Which member or service computes it in a consumer group, and what does every member need to send so that it can?
With an eager protocol every member stops consuming all its partitions at the start of a rebalance. How would you use your output to stop only the partitions that actually move?
Members have different capacity: some run on larger machines. How would you change the quotas, and does "fewest moves" still have a clean definition?
Partitions differ in traffic by a factor of 100. How would you balance load instead of counts without moving many more partitions on every rebalance?

rules.ask: Round robin from scratch is balanced. How many partitions does it move when one member joins a group of 50 members that owns 3 000 partitions, and what does each move cost a consumer with local state?
You scan the members for every free partition. How many steps is that with 150 000 free partitions and 4 000 members?
What exactly is your heap key, and what goes wrong if the member id is not part of it?
How can two members both report the same partition, and what would happen if both kept consuming it?
In a cooperative rebalance, partitions that move are revoked first and assigned in a second round. Using your output, which partitions are revoked from whom?

templates.title: Read-committed view of a partition — transactions, markers and the last stable offset
templates.subtopic: transactions, single-pass state machines

sections.scenario: Producers write to the {{topic}} topic inside transactions, so that a batch of related records becomes visible to consumers all at once or not at all. In one partition's log, transactional records from many producers are interleaved. When a transaction ends, a commit or abort marker for that producer is written to the log. Consumers that use read_committed must never see aborted records, and must not read past the first record of a transaction that is still open, because that transaction could still commit. A test tool needs to compute exactly which records such a consumer would receive, and a partition can hold hundreds of thousands of entries.
sections.problem:
Implement visible_records(log, high_watermark, start=0, isolation="read_committed"). log is a list of (offset, producer_id, kind) in increasing offset order. kind is "data" (a non-transactional record), "txn" (a transactional record), or "commit" / "abort" (a marker for that producer). Return, in order, the offsets of the records a consumer receives when it reads from offset start. These are this exercise's rules, modelled on the publicly documented behaviour; check current docs:

  1. Entries at or above high_watermark do not exist yet for consumers, and that includes markers.
  2. A producer's transaction is its run of "txn" records after its previous marker (or from the start of the log). The producer's next marker below the high watermark ends it, as committed or aborted. A marker when the producer has no open transaction changes nothing.
  3. read_uncommitted returns every "data" and "txn" record with start ≤ offset < high_watermark.
  4. read_committed reads only below the last stable offset: the first offset of the earliest transaction that is still open, or high_watermark if none is open. Below it, it returns every "data" record and every "txn" record of a committed transaction, with offset ≥ start.

Markers are never returned. {{replay_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 log entries from up to 1 000 producers. Offsets increase but can have gaps. Something close to O(n) is expected. Checking every record against every aborted transaction, or scanning ahead from each record to its marker, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Offsets, producer ids and volumes are hypothetical. One producer has at most one open transaction at a time. Non-transactional records never join a transaction, even when their producer has one open.
sections.criteria: Entries at or above the high watermark ignored, markers included; transactions defined per producer between markers, with stray markers ignored; the last stable offset taken from the earliest open transaction, even one that began before start; committed records above the last stable offset held back; non-transactional records cut at the last stable offset too; read_uncommitted returning aborted records; markers never returned; one O(n) sweep with per-producer state; good answers on hung transactions and batch-by-batch filtering.

clarifications.q: A transaction's commit marker is at the high watermark. Is it committed?
clarifications.a: Not yet. The marker is not visible, so the transaction is still open and it sets the last stable offset.

clarifications.q: Is a non-transactional record after the last stable offset returned?
clarifications.a: No. A read_committed consumer reads nothing at or after the last stable offset.

clarifications.q: A committed transaction has records both below and above the last stable offset. Which are returned?
clarifications.a: Only the ones below it. The others are returned later, once the open transaction ends.

clarifications.q: Does a transaction that began before start matter?
clarifications.a: Yes. If it is still open, the last stable offset is below start and nothing is returned.

clarifications.q: What does read_uncommitted do with aborted records?
clarifications.a: It returns them. It ignores transactions entirely, apart from never returning markers.

hints: Sweep the log once. For each producer, keep the offsets of its open transaction. On a marker, decide all of them at once, then forget the producer.
After the sweep, whatever is still open sets the last stable offset: take the smallest first offset among open transactions.
A second pass can then pick the visible offsets in order. There is no need to sort anything.
followups: A producer opens a transaction and then hangs. What do read_committed consumers of this partition see until the transaction times out, and which metric would show it?
Real consumers do not get the whole log at once. They get a batch and a list of aborted transactions with their first offsets. How would you filter batch by batch with bounded memory?
Your consumer reads the topic and writes results to another topic in the same transaction. What does that give you end to end, and what does it not give a database sink?
Compaction runs on a transactional topic. Which records and markers can it remove, and when?

rules.ask: You check every record against the list of aborted transactions. How many comparisons is that with 300 000 records and 7 000 aborted transactions?
You hold records back until their marker. How much memory can one long transaction pin, and what bounds it?
One producer opens a transaction and stops. What happens to the last stable offset, and to every read_committed consumer of this partition?
Why can a consumer not read past the high watermark, even with read_uncommitted?
The log is already in offset order. What does your sort cost, and what would it hide if the log were not in order?

templates.title: Debug the schema compatibility checker
templates.subtopic: compatibility modes, defaults, enums, optional fields

sections.scenario: Before a producer team registers a new version of the {{subject}} schema, a pre-merge check runs the new schema against the versions already registered, under the subject's compatibility mode. Several complaints point at the checker. Widening amount from int to long was rejected, but a change that narrowed a field was accepted and broke consumers. A new field with default 0 was rejected as having no default. Adding an enum symbol was rejected under FORWARD even though the old enum has a default symbol. A schema compatible with the latest version was rejected because of a version from two years ago. Making an optional field required passed the check, and old records with nulls then failed to read.
sections.problem:
Fix check_compatibility(new_schema, previous, mode) so that it meets this specification. These are this exercise's rules, a simplified model of the publicly documented Avro resolution rules and registry modes; check current docs. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Schemas. {"name": ..., "fields": [...]}. A field is {"name", "type"} plus, optionally, "default" (any value, including 0, "", False or None) and "optional": True (the field may hold null). A type is a primitive name ("boolean", "int", "long", "float", "double", "string", "bytes") or an enum {"enum": [symbols]} with an optional "default" symbol.
  2. Reading. A reader schema can read data written with a writer schema field by field. A reader field fails if the writer has no field of that name and the reader field has no "default" key. It also fails if the writer's field type cannot be read as the reader's type, or if the writer's field is optional and the reader's is not. Writer fields the reader does not have are ignored.
  3. Types. Two primitives are readable if they are equal or the writer's type promotes to the reader's: int → long, float, double; long → float, double; float → double; string ↔ bytes. Two enums are readable if every writer symbol is a reader symbol, or the reader's enum has a default symbol. An enum and a primitive are never readable.
  4. Modes. BACKWARD: the new schema must read data written with the latest version. FORWARD: the latest version must read data written with the new schema. FULL: both. The _TRANSITIVE forms check every registered version, not only the latest. NONE checks nothing.
  5. Output. previous is oldest first, and version v is previous[v - 1]. Return a sorted list of [version, direction, field], where direction is "backward" (the new schema cannot read that version's data) or "forward" (that version cannot read the new schema's data). Return [] when compatible, when the mode is NONE, or when nothing is registered.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 300 versions of 300 fields, in time linear in the fields checked.
sections.assumptions: Schemas are simplified and hypothetical: no nested records, unions other than optional, arrays, maps, aliases or logical types. Field names are unique within a schema.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom; promotion checked from writer type to reader type; default presence tested by key, not truthiness; enum default symbol honoured; non-transitive modes check the latest version; optional rule applied when the writer may send null and the reader cannot hold it; the fixes stay minimal; a regression test per bug; credible answers on renames, mode choice and failures the model misses.

clarifications.q: Is a default of None a default?
clarifications.a: Yes. The rule is whether the "default" key is present, not what its value is.

clarifications.q: Does an optional field without a default get null automatically when it is missing?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise, as in Avro, a field the reader never receives needs a declared default, optional or not.

clarifications.q: Which way does a promotion go?
clarifications.a: From the writer's type to the reader's. A reader declared long can read data written as int, not the other way round.

clarifications.q: For BACKWARD, which schema is the reader?
clarifications.a: The new one: consumers upgraded to it must read records already written with the old version.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: For each complaint, write the smallest pair of schemas that reproduces it, and decide which schema is the reader before you look at the code.
Read PROMOTIONS and its comment, then read how _type_ok uses it.
List the Python values that are falsy. Which of them are legitimate defaults?
previous is oldest first. Which element is the latest version?
followups: A team wants to rename a field. Under FULL_TRANSITIVE, what sequence of versions and deployments gets them there, and how long does it take?
The subject is BACKWARD, but a consumer still running an old schema reads new records. What breaks, and which mode should the subject have had?
Your checker says compatible, yet a consumer fails in production after the change. Name two ways that can happen that this model does not cover.
Several topics share one record type through references to another subject. How do you check a change to the shared type without breaking any of them?

rules.ask: Which defaults does if not rf.get("default") wrongly treat as missing? Give one for every primitive type.
Why do consumers that replay a topic from the beginning need a transitive mode, and what does it cost producers who want to evolve the schema?
Widening int to long passes BACKWARD. Does it pass FORWARD? Explain it with the reader and the writer.
Adding an enum symbol: which mode does it break when the old enum has no default symbol, and what do old consumers do with the new symbol?
Making a field optional is safe in one direction only. Which, and why?

templates.title: Consumer lag monitoring — offsets, time behind and alerts that do not flap
templates.subtopic: consumer lag in offsets and time, alerting state machines

sections.scenario: A streaming platform serves many teams, and each team runs consumer groups against shared clusters: about {{groups}} groups reading {{partitions}} partitions in total. Teams want to know when a group falls behind, but "lag" means different things to different groups. A batch-style sink that commits every ten minutes always shows a large offset lag and is fine. A payment consumer 2 000 records behind on a quiet topic may be hours late. Today one alert rule on offset lag pages people for healthy groups and misses stuck ones, and on-call has started to mute it. You are asked to design lag monitoring that teams trust, with a page when a group is {{page_after}}.
sections.problem: Design the system that measures and alerts on consumer lag. Cover what you collect and from where (log-end offsets, committed offsets, record timestamps) every {{sample_every}}; how you compute lag in offsets and lag in time per partition and roll it up per group; how you tell "behind but catching up" from "stuck" and from "idle topic"; how alerts are evaluated without flapping; how teams set thresholds per group; and how you keep collection cheap at this scale.
sections.constraints: Collection must not load the brokers noticeably. A group that has stopped committing must be detected even if its lag is small. Rebalances, which briefly stop commits, must not page anyone. Groups that are deleted or renamed must not leave stale alerts. Every alert must say which partitions are behind and since when.
sections.assumptions: Group counts, partition counts and thresholds are hypothetical. Committed offsets and log-end offsets can be read through the cluster's admin interface. Records carry timestamps, which may be producer-set and occasionally wrong.
sections.criteria: Both offset lag and time lag defined precisely, with the timestamp source and its failure modes; committed-offset progress tracked separately from lag, so stuck and idle groups are detected; window-based evaluation with hysteresis and minimum durations; rebalances and deleted groups handled; per-group thresholds with sane defaults; collection costed against broker load and series count; alerts that name partitions and onset; a clear answer for each follow-up.

clarifications.q: How is lag in time defined?
clarifications.a: You define it. Common choices are the age of the oldest unconsumed record (now minus the timestamp of the record at the committed offset), or offset lag divided by the recent consume rate. Say which and why.

clarifications.q: Does a consumer that commits rarely count as lagging?
clarifications.a: It should not page if it is keeping up. Your design has to tell that apart from one that is stuck.

clarifications.q: Who sets thresholds?
clarifications.a: Each owning team, per group, with defaults from the platform. Most teams will keep the default.

clarifications.q: Can you add code to the consumers?
clarifications.a: Not to all of them. Assume you see only what the cluster knows: offsets, commits, group membership and records.

hints: Lag in offsets is cheap and exact, but it means nothing without a rate. Lag in time is what people care about. Decide how you will get a timestamp for the committed position without reading too much.
Think in windows: over the last N samples, is the committed offset moving, and is lag shrinking, flat or growing?
Alert on a state that has held for a while, with separate thresholds to raise and to clear.
followups: A group's committed offset stays still for 20 minutes during a rebalance storm, then jumps. What did your system show and page during those 20 minutes?
A producer writes records with timestamps a day in the future. What does your lag in time show, and how do you protect against it?
A topic gets no new records for a weekend. Its consumer group stopped committing on Friday. Is it lagging?
Collection at {{partitions}} partitions every {{sample_every}} costs too much. What do you sample less often, and what do you lose?
Teams ask for a forecast: "when will this group catch up?". How would you compute it, and when should you not show it?

rules.ask: A group is 2 000 records behind on a topic that gets one record a minute, and another is 2 million behind on a topic that gets 100 000 a second. Which is worse, and how does your alert know?
Whose clock set that timestamp, and what does your time lag show when it is a day in the future or years in the past?
One threshold for every group pages the batch sinks every ten minutes. How do teams set their own, and what is the default?
Write down your raise and clear conditions. What does a group that hovers at the threshold do with them?
How many time series is that at {{partitions}} partitions, and which of them do you actually need to keep?

incidents: After a client library upgrade, about a third of the {{groups}} groups rebalance every few minutes for an hour, and their commits stall while their lag grows and shrinks.
One producer's clock is wrong, and a topic's records arrive stamped nine hours in the future.
The collector falls behind: one pass over {{partitions}} partitions now takes longer than {{sample_every}}, so samples arrive late and unevenly spaced.

templates.title: Dead-letter handling for sink connectors — tolerance, context and replay
templates.subtopic: error handling, dead-letter topics, replay and idempotent sinks

sink: an object store as Parquet files

sections.scenario: A platform team runs {{connectors}} sink connectors that copy topics into {{sink}}, about {{daily_records}} records a day. Sometimes records cannot be written: a producer ships a record whose schema the target does not accept, a field holds text where a number is expected, a value is too large for the target column, or the target briefly refuses writes. On a bad day about {{bad_rate}} of one topic's records fail. Today a connector either stops on the first bad record, which blocks every good record behind it, or is set to skip errors and silently drops data. Teams want bad records set aside with enough context to fix them, the good ones kept flowing, and a safe way to replay the fixed records.
sections.problem: Design error handling for the sink connector fleet. Cover which errors are retried and which are dead-lettered (transient target errors, conversion errors, transformation errors, records the target rejects); the dead-letter topic: naming, partitioning, retention, and the context stored with each record (source topic, partition, offset, error stage and class, connector, time); how tolerance is configured and when a connector should still stop; monitoring and alerting on dead-letter volume; and the replay process after a fix, including ordering, duplicates and how you prove the gap is closed.
sections.constraints: Good records must keep flowing when a bad one is dead-lettered. Nothing may be dropped without a record of it. Replay must not create duplicates in the target or reorder updates to the same key. Dead-lettered records may contain personal data and must follow the source topic's access rules and retention. A connector restart must not dead-letter the same record twice.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, rates and targets are hypothetical. As this exercise's rule, the connector framework can be configured to tolerate errors, route failed records to a dead-letter topic and attach error context as record headers, with retries for transient errors; which failure stages that covers depends on the framework version, so check current docs.
sections.criteria: Errors classified by stage and retryability, with transient errors retried and bounded; a dead-letter topic per connector or per source topic with clear ownership, access and retention; full context with every record (source coordinates, stage, error, time); tolerance with a rate guard that still stops a connector on a flood; alerts on dead-letter volume and age; replay that is idempotent, keeps per-key order and proves completeness by source offsets; personal data handled in dead-letter copies; good answers to the follow-ups.

clarifications.q: Should a target outage send records to the dead-letter topic?
clarifications.a: No. That would dead-letter everything. You decide how transient errors are retried, and how long before the connector stops.

clarifications.q: Who owns a dead-lettered record?
clarifications.a: The team that produces the topic usually owns the fix, and the platform owns the mechanism. Say how each finds out.

clarifications.q: Can the target take the same record twice?
clarifications.a: Only if your writes are idempotent, for example an upsert by key. An append-only target cannot, unless you deduplicate.

clarifications.q: Do updates to the same key need to stay in order?
clarifications.a: Yes, for keyed topics. A replayed old value must not overwrite a newer one.

hints: Classify errors by where they happen (converting, transforming, writing) and whether retrying can help. Only deterministic failures belong in the dead-letter topic.
The source topic, partition and offset are the record's identity. Keep them with the dead-lettered record, and you can replay, deduplicate and prove completeness.
For keyed upserts, a replayed record is only safe if the target can tell it is older than what it already holds.
followups: A producer deploys a bad change and {{bad_rate}} becomes 40% for an hour. What should happen, and what should stop?
The fix is in. Walk through replaying 2 million dead-lettered records into {{sink}} while the live connector keeps running.
A replayed record for key K is older than the value the target now holds for K. How do you stop it from overwriting newer data?
Legal asks you to delete one customer's records everywhere, including dead-letter topics and replay copies. What does your design make easy or hard?
How would you show each team, every morning, which of their records are not in the target and why?

rules.ask: With tolerance set to skip every error, what stops a bad deploy from dead-lettering half a topic without anyone noticing?
Which errors do you retry, for how long, and what does the connector do with the records behind the one it is retrying?
Your replay writes old records while the live connector writes new ones for the same keys. How does the target keep the newest value?
Which context do you store with each dead-lettered record, and which of it could leak personal data?
One shared dead-letter topic for {{connectors}} connectors: how does a team find and replay only its records, and who may read the others?

incidents: A producer deploy changes a field's type. Within ten minutes, 40% of one topic's records go to the dead-letter topic instead of the usual {{bad_rate}}.
The target, {{sink}}, refuses writes for 25 minutes during maintenance, and every connector writing to it starts to fail.
A replay of fixed records is started twice by mistake, from two terminals, while the live connector is running.

templates.title: Schema governance — subjects, versions, compatibility, owners, tags and approved breaking changes
templates.subtopic: schema registry metadata, ownership, field classification, change approval

sections.scenario: A company runs its event platform on Kafka with a schema registry in front of it, the kind of product Confluent documents publicly: producers register Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema definitions under subjects, each subject keeps numbered versions, and each new version is checked against a compatibility mode (backward, forward, full, their transitive variants, or none; in this exercise backward is the default, as the public docs describe; check current docs). There are about {{subjects}} subjects, owned by {{teams}} teams, and about {{pii_share}} of all fields hold personal data. Today ownership lives in a spreadsheet, classification in nobody's head, and a team that needs a breaking change sets its subject's compatibility to none for an afternoon. Governance wants every subject owned, every personal-data field tagged, and every breaking change (about {{breaking_requests}} requests a month) approved with a migration plan before it can land.
sections.problem: Design the governance data model that sits beside the registry, and the low-level flow of a schema change. Cover: the entities (subject, schema, subject version, compatibility setting and its history, owner team, field-level classification tags, known producers and consumers of a subject, change request, approval, exception) with their keys and how history is kept; how the model is fed from the registry and kept in sync; and how a change moves from proposal to registration, with which checks run where. Show how the model answers "which subjects with a personal-data field are read by teams other than the owner", "who changed the compatibility of subject X, when and under which approval", "which breaking changes were approved last quarter and which consumers have migrated", and "which schema version was current for topic T at time t".
sections.constraints: The registry stays the source of truth for schemas, ids and versions; the governance model never re-numbers or rewrites them. Configuration changes, approvals and tag changes are append-only and attributable to a person. A field's classification must follow the field from version to version. A subject deleted from the registry keeps its governance history. Nothing in the model requires reading message payloads.
sections.assumptions: Subject, team and request counts are hypothetical. Most subjects follow the default naming in which a topic's value schema is the subject <topic>-value and its key schema <topic>-key; some teams use record-name strategies. A schema id identifies a schema text and can appear under several subjects (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
sections.criteria: Registry facts mirrored append-only and never rewritten; subject-to-topic mapping explicit; compatibility history with actor and approval; field-path tags carried across versions with new fields unclassified by default; producer and consumer dependencies with a stated source of truth; a change flow that runs the compatibility check, classification check and approval before registration; exceptions with expiry; deletions recorded, not erased; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a subject the same thing as a topic?
clarifications.a: No. With the default naming they line up one to one; with record-name strategies one topic can carry several subjects and one subject can serve several topics. Model the mapping explicitly.

clarifications.q: Who may set compatibility to none?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, only an approved exception with an expiry time, recorded in your model.

clarifications.q: Do consumers register anywhere?
clarifications.a: Not in the registry. Build the dependency list from what you can observe (consumer groups reading the topic, schema ids fetched by clients) and from declarations, and say which one you trust.

clarifications.q: How is a field identified across versions?
clarifications.a: Your choice. A path within the record (for example customer.email) is the simplest; say how a rename is handled.

clarifications.q: Can a breaking change ever land on the same subject?
clarifications.a: Only with an approved request, a migration plan and every known consumer's acknowledgement; otherwise it goes to a new subject or topic.

hints: Mirror the registry's facts (subject, version, schema id, compatibility setting) as append-only rows fed by the registry, and keep governance (owners, tags, requests, approvals) in your own tables keyed by them.

Tag fields by path within a subject version and carry the tags forward when the path still exists; a field that is new in a version arrives unclassified and blocks or flags the change until it is reviewed.
A breaking-change request references the subject, the proposed schema, the compatibility check result, the approvers and the consumers that must acknowledge.
followups: Show the rows written when a team registers version 7 of orders-value, adding an optional field with a default, under backward compatibility.
A field tagged as personal data is renamed in a new version. How does the tag follow it, and what stops an untagged copy of the data from slipping through?
Someone sets the subject's compatibility to none at 02:00 and registers an incompatible schema. What does your model show the next morning, and what should have prevented it?
For a proposed change, produce the list of consumers that would break. Where does it come from, how stale can it be, and who signs off when a consumer is unknown?
Across {{subjects}} subjects, how do you keep governance and registry in sync, and what happens to a subject created directly in the registry, outside the process?

rules.ask: A team uses a record-name strategy so one topic carries three event types. How does your model map topics to subjects, and which compatibility setting protects that topic's consumers?
Who may set compatibility to none, for how long, and how does your model show every schema registered while it was in force?
Are your tags on the subject, the schema version or the field path? A new version adds a field holding an email address: what is its classification until someone reviews it?
Under the mode you chose, which side must upgrade first, producers or consumers, and where does your change flow record that order?

A version is deleted from the registry while retained messages still carry its schema id. What does your governance history keep, and how do you stop a deletion that would leave those messages unreadable?

incidents: A team set its subject's compatibility to none to ship a hotfix and registered a schema that removed a field without a default. Consumers in three other teams failed to deserialise for two hours, and governance showed nothing because configuration changes were never captured.

A classification sweep reports that {{pii_share}} of fields are tagged, but a new version renamed email to contact_email, the tag did not follow, and the field reached an analytics topic that every team can read.

With {{breaking_requests}} breaking-change requests a month waiting on review, teams start registering near-copies such as orders-value-v2-tmp to avoid the queue; within a quarter hundreds of subjects have no owner.

templates.title: Orders as events — keys, partitions, compacted state topics versus event topics, and the ordering you can promise
templates.subtopic: keys and partitioning, event versus state topics, envelopes, ordering and erasure

sections.scenario: An online marketplace is moving its order service onto Kafka. An order is created, items can be changed until payment, payment is authorised, the order is packed and shipped (possibly in several shipments), delivered, and may be cancelled or refunded. There are about {{orders_per_day}} orders a day, the planned orders topic has {{partitions}} partitions, and {{consumer_teams}} teams will consume it: fulfilment, notifications, fraud, finance and analytics among them. The largest merchant produces about {{hot_merchant_share}} of all order events. Some consumers want every change as it happened; others want the current state of each order, and a new service must be able to start without replaying years of history.
sections.problem: Design the topics and the events. Decide between, or combine, an event topic of typed order events and a compacted state topic holding each order's latest full state; give each topic's key, partitioning and partition count; define the envelope (event id, order id, per-order sequence, event time, producer, schema reference, correlation and causation ids) and where each field lives (key, headers or value); explain how the order service publishes so that a database commit and its event never disagree; state exactly which ordering guarantees consumers get and how they detect gaps, duplicates and stale updates; and describe how an order's personal data is erased from the compacted topic and what remains elsewhere.
sections.constraints: Every consumer sees one order's events in the order they happened. A consumer can rebuild current state from the state topic alone. Event ids are unique and consumers are idempotent. Increasing the partition count must not reorder in-flight orders, or you say how the change is made safely. Personal data must be removable on request.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and team counts are hypothetical. In this exercise the producer's default partitioner hashes the key bytes and takes the result modulo the partition count, and a compacted topic keeps at least the latest value per key, with a tombstone (a null value) kept for delete.retention.ms before it is removed (this exercise's rules; check current docs). An order's id, merchant and customer never change after creation.
sections.criteria: Order id as the key with the reason stated; event and state topics distinguished, with the state topic compacted and derivable; an envelope with event id, per-order sequence and schema reference; an atomic publish path (outbox or CDC) with the crash case handled; ordering promised per order only, with gap and duplicate handling in consumers; a safe plan for changing the partition count; tombstones and retention explained for erasure, including copies outside Kafka; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Must events of different orders be ordered relative to each other?
clarifications.a: No. Only one order's events. The notifications team would like one customer's orders in order; decide whether you support it.

clarifications.q: Can the service write to its database and to Kafka in one transaction?
clarifications.a: Not across both systems. Choose an outbox, change data capture from the order tables, or Kafka as the log of record, and say what happens on a crash between the two writes.

clarifications.q: Does the largest merchant need its own ordering?
clarifications.a: No. Its orders are independent of one another.

clarifications.q: How long are events kept?
clarifications.a: The event topic keeps 30 days in this exercise; the state topic is compacted and kept indefinitely; longer history lives in the warehouse.

clarifications.q: Can a consumer ask for a single order's history?
clarifications.a: Not from Kafka efficiently. Say where that query is served.

hints: Per-order ordering comes from one order always landing on one partition, so key by order id. Keying by merchant puts the largest merchant's {{hot_merchant_share}} of events on one partition.
Separate "what happened" (typed events) from "what is true now" (full latest state per order, compacted). A stream processor can derive the second from the first.
A per-order sequence number in every event lets consumers detect gaps, duplicates and stale updates without trusting delivery alone.
followups: Write the envelope and two events, OrderCreated and ShipmentDispatched, with their keys. What goes in the key, in headers and in the value?
The notifications team needs a customer's orders in order. With order-id keys, how do they get it, and what does it cost?
The topic must grow from {{partitions}} partitions to twice that. What happens to orders in flight, and how would you migrate without breaking per-order ordering?
A customer asks to be erased. What do you write to the state topic, when is the old value really gone, and what about the event topic and every consumer's copy?

Without idempotence, with retries and several requests in flight, two events of one order can be written out of order. Which producer settings prevent it, and how does the sequence number protect a consumer anyway?

rules.ask: The largest merchant produces {{hot_merchant_share}} of events. What does keying by merchant do to one partition and to every consumer's lag during its sale?
Without a key, two events of one order land on different partitions. What does a consumer do when it sees "shipped" before "created"?
Who reads the outbox table, and what happens if the relay crashes after publishing a batch but before marking those rows sent?
A new service bootstraps from the compacted topic. What does it see for an erased order, and for an order whose last two updates are still in the uncompacted part of the log?
One partition gives a total order. What throughput ceiling and failure blast radius does that impose at {{orders_per_day}} orders a day?

incidents: After a deploy, the outbox relay republished a batch of order events. Consumers that did not deduplicate by event id sent customers a second "your order has shipped" message.

A team re-keyed its copy of the state topic by merchant id to simplify merchant dashboards. During the largest merchant's sale one of the {{partitions}} partitions carried its {{hot_merchant_share}} of traffic, and that partition's consumers fell hours behind.

An operator doubled the partition count in production without a migration plan. For a few thousand in-flight orders, later events hashed to a different partition, and fulfilment processed "delivered" before "shipped".

templates.title: Cluster metadata as history — brokers, topics, partitions and replica assignments over time
templates.subtopic: interval history of brokers, topics, assignments, leaders and ISR for capacity and placement

sections.scenario: A platform team runs a fleet of Kafka clusters: {{clusters}} clusters, {{brokers}} brokers and about {{replicas}} partition replicas in total. The metadata keeps changing: brokers are added, decommissioned and rebuilt in another rack; topics are created, deleted and sometimes recreated under the same name; partition counts grow; configurations such as retention and minimum in-sync replicas change; reassignments move replicas between brokers; leaders move and in-sync replica sets shrink and expand. Capacity planners and on-call engineers ask questions about the past: which brokers held replicas of a topic on a date, disk per broker per day against what was assigned to it, how many partitions had every replica in one rack last month, how leadership was spread across brokers over time, and which reassignments were running when produce latency rose. A collector can read the metadata through the admin interface every {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes.
sections.problem: Design the history model and how it is captured. Cover: stable identities (cluster, broker, topic, partition) versus the facts that change about them (rack, configuration, replica assignment with its order, leader, in-sync replicas, replica size per log directory); how a topic recreated under the same name stays distinct from its predecessor; how history is stored (validity intervals, a change log, periodic snapshots, or a mix) and why; how a reassignment in progress is represented; the daily capacity fact and its grain; how as-of questions are answered efficiently; and what the model records when the collector misses snapshots.
sections.constraints: Any as-of question for the last 13 months is answerable at the snapshot interval's precision. A topic deleted and recreated under the same name is never merged with its predecessor. Replica order is kept, because the first replica is the preferred leader. Storage is bounded: estimate a full snapshot every {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes for 13 months and justify what you keep instead. A gap in collection is never recorded as a change that did not happen.
sections.assumptions: Fleet sizes are hypothetical. Clusters run without ZooKeeper (KRaft mode) and give each topic a unique topic id in addition to its name (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Each broker reports the size of each replica it hosts. Collector clocks are synchronised.
sections.criteria: Identities separated from changing facts, with topics keyed by topic id and the name kept as an attribute; validity intervals (or change log plus periodic checkpoints) with a storage estimate; replica order and preferred leader kept; reassignments represented explicitly; a daily capacity fact at a stated grain; as-of queries with suitable clustering; collection gaps recorded as unknown, never as change; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can I key topics by name?
clarifications.a: Not safely. A topic can be deleted and recreated under the same name with a different partition count. Decide how you key it.

clarifications.q: How do I recognise a reassignment in the data?
clarifications.a: While it runs, a partition lists replicas being added and replicas being removed next to its target assignment; it ends when the target replicas are in sync and the removed ones are gone.

clarifications.q: Do we need in-sync replica history at full precision?
clarifications.a: It changes often during incidents. Keep it, and say at what grain and for how long.

clarifications.q: Are racks fixed?
clarifications.a: No. A broker can come back in another rack after a rebuild; placement questions use the rack at the time.

clarifications.q: Will snapshots be missed?
clarifications.a: Yes. The collector restarts, and a cluster can be unreachable for an hour.

hints: Separate identities from changing facts, and give each fact a valid_from and valid_to; most questions become "intervals that overlap time t".
Diff consecutive snapshots into change rows instead of storing every snapshot; a missed snapshot leaves an interval's end uncertain rather than inventing a change.
Capacity questions want one cheap daily fact (replica × day with bytes, leader flag and rack) that aggregates to broker, rack and topic.
followups: Sketch the as-of query for "replicas of topic T on brokers in rack R at time t". Which clustering or index makes it fast?
Estimate a year of full snapshots of {{replicas}} replicas every {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes against change intervals. What do you keep for 13 months, and at which grain?
A topic is deleted and recreated under the same name with more partitions. Show the rows, and how "bytes per topic per day" avoids mixing them.
The collector missed 50 minutes on one cluster while a reassignment ran. What does your model record for that gap, and what does it refuse to claim?
A planner asks which brokers have led more than their fair share of partitions, and since when. Which tables answer it, and how do preferred-leader elections show up?

rules.ask: The topic was deleted and recreated under the same name an hour later. Which rows does your key merge, and what does the capacity chart show for that day?
At {{replicas}} replicas every {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes, how many rows is that in a year, and what do you keep at that grain?
How do you close an interval when the collector misses snapshots, and what does valid_to say while a change is unconfirmed?
Is the leader part of the assignment row or a separate fact? How do you show preferred versus actual leader over time?
A broker came back in a different rack after a rebuild. Does last month's placement check use today's rack or the rack at the time, and where does that come from in your model?

incidents: The day after a topic was recreated under the same name, a capacity report showed one broker at 140% of its disk: the old and new topics' replica sizes were summed under one key.

During a reassignment on the largest cluster, the collector's metadata call timed out and it wrote empty replica lists. History showed thousands of partitions with no replicas for {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes at a time, and the rack-spread alert paged.
A quarterly placement audit flagged partitions with every replica in one rack, but those brokers had been re-racked since; the audit joined history to today's broker table.

templates.title: Enriching payments with customer profiles — co-partitioning, repartition topics, changelog state and restore
templates.subtopic: stream–table join, co-partitioning, repartition and changelog topics, state restore

sections.scenario: A payments company scores every payment for fraud. A stream processing application (in the style of Kafka Streams, the open-source library) reads the payments topic, keyed by payment id, with {{partitions}} partitions and about {{events_per_sec}} events a second, and joins each payment to its customer's profile. Profiles come from change data capture of the customer database into a compacted customer-profiles topic keyed by customer id, about {{profiles}} customers, with a different partition count. The joined result, payments-enriched, feeds the fraud model. The table's local state is about {{state_gb}} GB across all instances, backed by a changelog topic. Fraud scoring tolerates a few minutes of delay at most.
sections.problem: Design the topology at a low level. Cover: re-keying payments by customer id and the repartition topic it needs (key, serialisation, partition count); the co-partitioning requirements of a stream–table join and how you meet them; the join's semantics (which side triggers output, which profile a payment sees, what happens when the profile does not exist yet, and guest payments with no customer id); a partitioned table versus a table copied to every instance; the state store, its changelog topic and how long a restore takes; standby replicas; and what you put in each enriched record so fraud scoring knows which profile version, if any, was used. Say how close a reprocessing from an earlier offset comes to the first run's result.
sections.constraints: Every payment yields exactly one enriched record, with or without a profile. The payments topic's key cannot change, because other consumers rely on it. One instance failing must not stall scoring beyond your stated target. Keys on both sides of the join must be serialised identically.
sections.assumptions: Rates, sizes and partition counts are hypothetical. In this exercise the default partitioner hashes the serialised key bytes, so the same key serialised differently can land on a different partition (this exercise's rule; check current docs). A few percent of profiles change each day, in bursts after batch updates, and some profiles are created seconds before the customer's first payment.
sections.criteria: Re-keying through a repartition topic sized and serialised to match the table; co-partitioning stated precisely (key, serialisation, partitioner, partition count); join semantics correct (stream side triggers, table looked up, left join with a flag for missing profiles and guests); partitioned versus copied table weighed with numbers; changelog-backed state with a restore estimate, standbys and persistent state; profile version recorded in the output; reprocessing reproducibility discussed honestly; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can the profiles topic be re-partitioned?
clarifications.a: Not quickly; other applications read it. You may copy it inside your application.

clarifications.q: What should happen if the profile arrives after the payment?
clarifications.a: Your choice: emit with empty profile fields and a flag, or wait a bounded time. State the cost for fraud scoring.

clarifications.q: Which profile should a payment see on reprocessing?
clarifications.a: Ideally the one current at the payment's event time. Say whether your design achieves that or only approximates it.

clarifications.q: Can a payment have no customer id?
clarifications.a: Yes, guest checkouts. They still need an enriched record.

clarifications.q: Can I call the customer database for each payment instead?
clarifications.a: You may propose it; size the load and say what happens when the database slows down.

hints: A stream–table join runs locally per partition, so both inputs must be keyed by the join key, with the same partition count and the same partitioner. Re-keying the stream writes it through a repartition topic.
The table's state store is restored from a compacted changelog; a large store takes minutes to restore on a fresh instance, and standby replicas or a persistent state directory shorten that.
