A table copied to every instance removes the co-partitioning requirement, at the cost of holding all {{profiles}} profiles on each instance.
followups: Draw the topology with every internal topic (repartition and changelog), its key, partition count and cleanup policy.
The profiles topic has a different partition count from your repartition topic. What happens if you join them directly, and what are your options?
One instance dies. Estimate the restore time for its share of {{state_gb}} GB, and how standby replicas change that.
A payment arrives two seconds before its customer's profile. What does your join emit, and how does fraud scoring know the enrichment was incomplete?
Reprocessing last week's payments from an earlier offset gives different enrichment from the first run. Why, and what would make it reproducible?

rules.ask: At {{profiles}} customers, every instance holds the whole table. What does that cost per instance, and how long does a restart take to rebuild it?
How many partitions does your repartition topic have, which key serialiser does it use, and what happens to the order of one customer's payments?
Guest checkouts and payments that arrive before their profile disappear with an inner join. What does fraud scoring then never see?
How many standbys, on which instances, and what happens to restore time when a standby is far behind?
At {{events_per_sec}} events a second, what load does a per-payment lookup put on the customer database, and what happens to the stream when the database slows down?

incidents: A deploy changed how the customer id was serialised in the repartition topic (a string became a typed key). Partition counts still matched, but the same customer now hashed to a different partition, and enrichment returned no profile for most payments for an hour.

An instance restart restored its share of {{state_gb}} GB from the changelog because the state directory was on an ephemeral disk and no standby existed; fraud scoring on those partitions fell 40 minutes behind.

A reprocessing job rebuilt last month's enriched payments for a fraud-model backtest. It joined them to today's profiles, and the model learned from information it would not have had at the time of each payment.

templates.title: Mirror lag by the hour — offset lag and time lag per mirrored partition from two samplers
templates.subtopic: as-of lookups between two sampled series, first-crossing time, arg-max per group

sections.scenario: A platform team replicates topics from a source Kafka cluster to other clusters with cluster links. {{links_rule}} In this exercise a link keeps offsets: a mirrored record has the same offset in the mirror partition as in its source partition (this exercise's rule; check current docs), so the two log-end offsets can be compared directly. Two samplers run independently between {{window_start}} and {{window_end}}: source_offsets records each source partition's log-end offset, and mirror_offsets records, per link, the log-end offset of every partition on that link's destination cluster. Their clocks agree, but their sampling times do not. {{naming_rule}} The on-call team wants, for every hour, how far each link's mirrors are behind, in records and in time.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns link_name, topic, hour_start, max_offset_lag, max_time_lag_s, worst_partition. Evaluate every destination sample that is the mirror of a source topic; its source partition has that source topic and the same partition_id. Let L be the log_end_offset of the latest source sample of that partition taken at or before the destination sample's sampled_at; a destination sample with no such source sample is not evaluated. offset_lag is L minus the destination sample's log_end_offset, floored at 0. time_lag_s is 0 when offset_lag is 0; otherwise it is the whole number of seconds from the earliest source sample of that partition whose log_end_offset is greater than the destination sample's log_end_offset, to the destination sample's sampled_at. Group the evaluated samples by link, source topic and the UTC hour of the destination sample's sampled_at (hour_start is the start of that hour). max_offset_lag and max_time_lag_s are the maxima over the group; worst_partition is the partition_id of the sample with the largest time lag (ties go to the smaller partition_id), or NULL when max_time_lag_s is 0. Order by link_name, topic, hour_start.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). "At or before" is inclusive, and a sample taken at exactly hh:00:00 belongs to the hour that starts then. Offsets in a partition never decrease. The sample has {{source_rows}} source samples and {{mirror_rows}} destination samples; production samples tens of thousands of partitions every few seconds.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical clusters, topics, offsets and times. Both samplers' clocks are synchronised. The time lag is a sampled estimate: the record at the mirror's log-end offset was appended at or before the first source sample that showed it, so the true lag is at least this value and less than the time since the source sample before that one.
sections.criteria: An as-of lookup (latest source sample at or before each destination sample) instead of an equality join or the newest sample; offset lag floored at 0; time lag from the earliest source sample with a higher offset, 0 when caught up; destination samples with no earlier source sample left out; hours bucketed with date_trunc on the destination time; worst partition by time lag with the tie rule and NULL when nothing is behind; at the hardest level, the link prefix stripped exactly and only from the start, so dotted names and destination-local topics are handled; can explain the sampling uncertainty and how to run this continuously.

clarifications.q: Does a source sample taken at exactly the destination sample's time count as at or before it?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is the latest one at or before.

clarifications.q: The destination is sometimes ahead of the latest source sample. Is that an error?
clarifications.a: No. The source was sampled earlier and more records were produced and mirrored since. The offset lag is floored at 0 and the time lag is 0.

clarifications.q: Can the earliest source sample with a higher offset be in an earlier hour?
clarifications.a: Yes. The time lag can span hours; only the destination sample's time decides its group.

clarifications.q: Should an hour with samples but no lag appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with 0, 0 and NULL. An hour whose destination samples all predate the first source sample of their partitions does not appear.

clarifications.q: What is mirror_links for?
clarifications.a: It holds each link's topic_prefix, which maps a destination topic name to its source topic.

hints: For each destination sample, fetch the latest source sample of its partition at or before it with a LATERAL subquery (ORDER BY sampled_at DESC LIMIT 1); an inner lateral join drops the samples with nothing to compare against.
The earliest source sample with a higher log-end offset is a second lookup: MIN(sampled_at) over that partition's source samples whose log_end_offset exceeds the mirror's.
Number the samples in each group by time lag descending, then partition_id, to find the worst partition, then aggregate.
followups: The true time lag lies between your value and the time since the previous source sample. How would you report that uncertainty, and how would record timestamps change the approach?
At tens of thousands of partitions sampled every few seconds, how would you compute this continuously instead of with a lookup per destination sample?
Write an alert that fires when max_time_lag_s stays above 300 for three consecutive hours. What does it do for a link that was paused on purpose?
A link that does not keep offsets (a replication tool that translates them) is added. What extra data do you need, and which of these numbers still mean anything?

rules.ask: The two samplers almost never fire at the same instant. How many destination samples does an equality join on sampled_at keep, and what should the join condition be?
Is that the latest source sample before this destination sample, or the latest in the whole table? Show where your query compares the two times.
A window function orders one table. How do you get the source offset in force at each destination sample from a window over both samplers, and what happens when two samples share a timestamp?

The plain link has no prefix and some topic names contain dots. What does your expression return for a dotted topic name on that link, and for a destination-local topic that shares a name with a source topic?
One partition is 40 minutes behind while seven are current. What does an average across partitions show the on-call engineer, and why does this report use the maximum?

incidents: The source sampler stalled for 20 minutes during a broker restart while the links kept mirroring. Destination samples ran ahead of the last source sample, and a dashboard that averaged unfloored lag across partitions showed a link as healthy while one partition was far behind.

A link stopped replicating one partition during a quiet hour on its topic. Nothing new was produced, so offset lag and time lag both stayed 0 for that hour; the alert fired only once traffic resumed, and the on-call team asked why the report had looked healthy.

templates.title: Tiered storage: old log segments in object storage, historical reads, retention and cost
templates.subtopic: tiered log storage, remote reads, retention, cost

sections.scenario: A managed streaming service runs Kafka clusters for many customers. One cluster of {{brokers}} brokers takes in {{daily_ingest}} a day after replication is excluded. Customers want topics kept for {{retention_days}} days so that a new service can rebuild its state by replaying history, but broker disks are sized to hold only about {{local_hours}} hours of data. The plan is to keep the most recent data on broker disks and move older log segments to object storage, while every consumer keeps using the same topic, the same offsets and the same client API.
sections.problem: Design tiered storage for this cluster. Cover which segments become eligible to move and when; who uploads them and how a leader change is handled; the metadata that records which offset ranges live where; the read path for a consumer asking for an old offset, and how those reads are kept from hurting producers and consumers near the head of the log; retention and deletion in both tiers; what happens when object storage is slow or unavailable; and the cost model (storage, requests, network). Say which kinds of topics you would not tier and why.
sections.constraints: A segment must never be deleted from broker disk until its copy in object storage is complete and recorded. Producer p99 latency and head-of-log consumer latency must not change while customers replay history. Offsets must stay identical whichever tier serves a read. Object storage charges per request as well as per byte stored, and has per-prefix request-rate limits (hypothetical figures are fine).
sections.assumptions: All volumes and limits are hypothetical. Topics are replicated three ways across availability zones on broker disks; the object store is durable on its own and is not replicated by the brokers. For this exercise, only closed (rolled) segments whose records are all below the high watermark may be uploaded, and compacted topics are not tiered; this exercise's rules, check current docs.
sections.criteria: Clear eligibility rule (closed segments below the high watermark) and a single uploader per partition (the leader) with leader-epoch fencing; remote segment metadata with offset and time ranges, epochs and states (copy started, copy finished, delete started, deleted), so partial uploads and orphans are detectable; local deletion only after the remote copy is recorded; a separate, quota-limited historical read path with its own threads and cache so tail latency is protected; retention enforced from metadata in both tiers, with orphan clean-up; explicit behaviour when the object store fails (local retention extends, alerts on disk headroom, back-pressure as a last resort); a costed model including request counts; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does every replica upload its own copy?
clarifications.a: No. Only one copy per segment should exist in object storage; you decide which broker uploads it.

clarifications.q: Do consumers need to know which tier they are reading?
clarifications.a: No. The client API and offsets are unchanged; only latency differs.

clarifications.q: How often do customers replay full history?
clarifications.a: A few times a day across the cluster, often by dozens of consumers in parallel when a new service is launched.

clarifications.q: Can retention be changed on a live topic?
clarifications.a: Yes, up or down, at any time.

clarifications.q: Is there a budget?
clarifications.a: Yes. Show the main cost lines per day at the stated ingest and retention.

hints: Separate the log into an active part the brokers own and an immutable part described by metadata. Each remote segment needs its offset range, its time range and the leader epoch that wrote it.
Historical reads have very different I/O from tail reads. Give them their own threads, their own cache and their own quota.
Work out the request count, not just the bytes: segment size decides how many objects you create, list and fetch.
followups: Walk through one segment's life from being rolled on the leader to being deleted from object storage, naming every state change and the record of it.
The leader changes while a segment upload is half done. What does the new leader do, and how do you avoid two different objects claiming the same offsets?
Fifty consumers start reading the same topic from offset 0. How do you keep producer latency flat, and how do you avoid fetching the same objects fifty times?
A customer cuts retention from {{retention_days}} days to 7. How is the remote data removed, how fast, and how do you know nothing is left behind?
Object storage is unavailable for an hour. What happens to producers, to local disks sized for {{local_hours}} hours, and to consumers reading history?

rules.ask: Fifty replaying consumers each read a different part of the topic. What is your cache hit rate now, and what bounds the memory and disk it takes on each broker?
If followers also upload, how many copies of each segment do you pay for, and which one is authoritative when they differ?
Why is a compacted topic harder to tier than a time-retained one? What would have to change to support it?
Halve the segment size. What happens to request costs, to the number of metadata entries, and to how stale the remote tier is?
Who gets throttled first when historical reads and tail reads compete on one broker, and what does the customer see?

incidents: A customer launches a new service that starts 80 consumers from the beginning of a {{retention_days}}-day topic. Within minutes, request-handler threads on six brokers are busy waiting on object-storage reads, and producer p99 on those brokers rises from 8 ms to 900 ms.
Object storage in the cluster's region returns errors for 50 minutes. Uploads fail and back off, and broker disks, sized for about {{local_hours}} hours, keep filling; two brokers pass 90% disk.

After a run of leader elections, the storage bill for one large topic is 1.7 times what its retention predicts: the object store holds several copies of the same offset ranges that the metadata no longer references.
A topic's retention is cut from {{retention_days}} days to 7, and a week later the object store still holds almost all of the old data.

templates.title: Cross-region replication and failover: offsets, consumer groups, active-passive versus active-active
templates.subtopic: cross-region replication, offset translation, failover and failback

sections.scenario: A company runs its event streams on a Kafka cluster in one cloud region: {{topics}} topics, read by {{groups}} consumer groups, with orders, inventory and payment events among them. It wants a second region that can take over if the first is lost, with at most {{rpo_seconds}} seconds of committed records lost and service restored within {{rto_minutes}} minutes. Some teams also want to produce in both regions at once, so that users near each region get lower latency.
sections.problem: Design cross-region replication and failover. Cover how records, topic configurations, schemas and access rules reach the second region; how consumer group positions are carried over (whether offsets are preserved or translated, and what a consumer does with each); the failover procedure for producers and consumers, and who decides to fail over; failback once the first region returns; and how you measure replication lag in records and in time. Then compare active-passive with active-active for these workloads: topic naming, loop prevention, per-key ordering, and which applications can safely use each.
sections.constraints: Recovery point at most {{rpo_seconds}} seconds and recovery time at most {{rto_minutes}} minutes for the critical topics. Consumers must not skip records on failover; reprocessing some records is acceptable only for consumers that can handle duplicates, and you must say which. Cross-region network is billed per byte.
sections.assumptions: All counts and objectives are hypothetical. For this exercise, there are two kinds of replication tool: one that keeps the same offsets on the destination topic, and one that writes records with new offsets and publishes periodic checkpoints that map a group's source offset to a destination offset. This exercise's rules; check current docs for any product's behaviour.
sections.criteria: Replicates data, configurations, schemas (with the same ids) and access rules; explains offset preservation versus translation and their consequences for each kind of consumer; failover procedure with a decision owner, fencing of the old region and client redirection within {{rto_minutes}} minutes; failback that reconciles divergent writes rather than overwriting them; lag measured in time against {{rpo_seconds}} seconds; active-active only with per-key or per-topic ownership, origin tagging or prefixes to stop loops, and consumers that read both; regular drills that prove the objectives; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is replication synchronous?
clarifications.a: No. It is asynchronous; a synchronous stretch cluster is out of scope because of the distance.

clarifications.q: Do all topics need the same objectives?
clarifications.a: No. About a tenth are critical; the rest can tolerate hours.

clarifications.q: Are consumers idempotent?
clarifications.a: Some are (they upsert by key); some are not (they send emails or move money). You must say how each kind fails over.

clarifications.q: Who triggers failover?
clarifications.a: Your design should say: automatic, a human with a runbook, or automatic with a human gate.

clarifications.q: Does the schema registry need to be in both regions?
clarifications.a: Yes, with the same schema ids, or consumers in the second region cannot read the records.

hints: Start from what a consumer needs after failover: a position in the destination topic that is not ahead of what it had processed.
Measure lag in time as well as offsets; your objective is stated in seconds.
In active-active, decide which region owns each key or each topic. Two writers for one key across regions give you no ordering.
followups: A consumer group committed offset 1,000,000 in the first region. With each replication tool, where does it start in the second region, and what does it see again or miss?
Walk through a failover for one critical topic, minute by minute, against {{rto_minutes}} minutes.
The first region comes back after three hours. How do you fail back without losing what was written in the second region and without replaying everything twice?
Two teams want active-active for an inventory topic. What would have to be true of their keys and their consumers for that to be safe?
How do you prove, every week and without an outage, that you still meet {{rpo_seconds}} seconds and {{rto_minutes}} minutes?

rules.ask: Checkpoints are emitted every so often. How far behind can a translated position be, and which consumers can afford that many duplicates?
The same key is updated in both regions within a second. Which update wins, and how does every consumer in both regions agree?
Some producers cache the old cluster's broker addresses. How long do they keep writing to a dead region, and what happens to those records?
A network partition makes the first region look dead from the second, but it is still serving most users. What stops your automation from creating two primaries?
Consumers now have to read two topic names for one stream. How do they keep per-key order across both?

incidents: In a failover drill, consumers in the second region start from translated positions up to 90 seconds behind where they were, and a non-idempotent notification service sends about 40,000 duplicate messages to customers.

A new replication flow is set up between the two regions with the same topic names on both sides and no check on where a record came from. Records start cycling between the regions and the topic's byte rate doubles every few minutes.

The first region is lost and the second takes over. When the first returns, it holds records written in the last {{rpo_seconds}} seconds before the outage that never reached the second region, and some conflict with writes made since.
Replication lag for the critical topics is reported as 2,000 records, which looks healthy, but at night that is 9 minutes of data on a low-volume payments topic, far beyond {{rpo_seconds}} seconds.

templates.title: Exactly-once stream processing end to end, including sinks that are not transactional
templates.subtopic: transactions, read-committed consumers, idempotent sinks

sink: a partner's HTTP API that has no idempotency key

sections.scenario: An advertising platform bills advertisers per click. Click events arrive on a topic with {{partitions}} partitions at {{events_per_sec}} events per second. A stream processing application removes duplicate clicks, aggregates spend per advertiser per minute, and writes the results to an output topic. From there, results go to the billing ledger (another topic), and to {{sink}}. Finance says every click must be billed exactly once; a missed click is lost revenue and a double-billed one is a refund and a complaint.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline so that each click affects billing exactly once, end to end. Cover the producer side (retries and duplicates), the processing side (reading input, updating state, writing output and committing input positions as one unit), how a crashed or paused instance is stopped from writing after it has been replaced, what downstream consumers of the output topic must do to see only committed results, and how {{sink}} receives each result exactly once in effect, even though it does not take part in the topic's transactions. Explain the latency cost of committing every {{commit_ms}} ms.
sections.constraints: Results must be visible to billing within 30 seconds. Instances crash, pause for garbage collection and are rescheduled. The output topic is also read by teams you do not control. Input producers are mobile and web clients that retry on timeout.
sections.assumptions: All rates are hypothetical. For this exercise: an idempotent producer lets the broker drop retried duplicates within one producer session per partition; a transactional producer can write to several partitions and commit consumer positions atomically; a consumer in read_committed mode reads only up to the last stable offset (the first offset of a transaction still open), and skips records of aborted transactions; a producer that starts with the same transactional id fences older instances. This exercise's rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Separates input duplicates (dedup by click id within a bounded window, state in a changelog-backed store), retry duplicates (idempotent producer) and restart duplicates (consume-transform-produce in one transaction with input positions committed atomically); zombie fencing through a stable transactional id and epochs; consumers of the output in read_committed mode, with the cost of open transactions on the last stable offset explained; sink writes made idempotent (deterministic keys, upserts, or positions stored with the data) or an explicit dedup layer for an API with no idempotency key; commit interval chosen against latency and overhead; end-to-end reconciliation counts; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do clicks carry an id?
clarifications.a: Yes, a client-generated click id; the same click retried keeps its id.

clarifications.q: How long can a duplicate click arrive after the original?
clarifications.a: Almost always within 10 minutes; rarely up to an hour.

clarifications.q: Do the teams reading the output topic use read_committed?
clarifications.a: Some do not, and you cannot force them on day one.

clarifications.q: Can the sink be changed?
clarifications.a: You can change how you write to it, not the sink itself.

hints: Separate three problems: duplicates in the input, duplicates caused by your own retries and restarts, and duplicates at the sink.
Commit the input positions in the same transaction as the outputs; otherwise a crash between them replays or skips.
A sink that cannot join the transaction needs an idempotent write: a deterministic key per result, or the input positions stored alongside the data.
followups: Trace one click from the client retry to the billing ledger, naming each place a duplicate could be created and what removes it.
An instance pauses for longer than the transaction timeout and a replacement takes over its partitions. What happens when the paused instance wakes up and tries to commit?
What does a consumer of the output topic that does not use read_committed see, and what would you tell its team?
How do you deliver each result once in effect to {{sink}}? What breaks if the sink is down for 20 minutes?
Billing finds a 0.02% difference between clicks and billed clicks for one day. How do you find where it came from?

rules.ask: The client app retries a click after its process restarted. Does the idempotent producer catch that duplicate? What does?
Commit every 10 ms instead. What happens to throughput, to the number of transaction markers, and to brokers?
What exactly is the key, and does it stay the same if a window is recomputed after a late click?
Which component coordinates, what happens if it crashes between the two phases, and do you really need it here?
How big is your dedup state at {{events_per_sec}} events per second with a one-hour window, and where does it live when an instance moves?

incidents: A processing instance stops for 90 seconds in a garbage-collection pause, longer than the transaction timeout. Its partitions are reassigned; when it resumes, it tries to send its buffered results and commit.
A bug leaves one producer's transaction open for 15 minutes. read_committed consumers of the output topic report growing lag on three partitions although records are arriving.
The sink is unreachable for 20 minutes. When it comes back, results for those minutes are written twice because the writer inserts rows rather than writing by key.

After a deploy that raised the commit interval from {{commit_ms}} ms to 60 seconds, the billing dashboard shows spend arriving in one-minute steps and an advertiser's budget cap is overshot before the pacing service sees it.

templates.title: Managed connector fleet: scheduling thousands of tasks, isolation, status and restarts
templates.subtopic: multi-tenant scheduling, failure isolation, control plane

sections.scenario: A managed streaming service offers connectors: customers pick a plugin (one of {{plugins}} source and sink types, such as databases, object stores and SaaS APIs), give it a configuration and credentials, and the service runs it. Across {{tenants}} tenants there are {{tasks}} connector tasks running at once. Each task copies data between one external system and one or more topics. Customers see each connector's state (running, paused, failed) and want it within {{status_seconds}} seconds of a change.
sections.problem: Design the connector fleet. Cover the control plane (connector configurations, desired state, secrets) and the data plane (workers that run tasks); how tasks are placed on workers, and whether tenants share workers; how one tenant's failing or misbehaving task is kept from affecting others; restarts with backoff and when to stop restarting; where each task's source or sink positions are stored; how plugin versions are rolled out; how status and errors reach customers; and capacity planning as tasks are added and removed.
sections.constraints: A failure in one tenant's connector must not stop or slow another tenant's. Credentials must never appear in logs or status messages. Changing one connector must not pause unrelated tasks. A plugin version must be rollable back within minutes.
sections.assumptions: All counts are hypothetical. For this exercise, a connector is split into tasks, each task's progress is stored as positions in a topic or store the service owns, and workers in one group rebalance tasks among themselves when members change. This exercise's model; check current docs for any product's behaviour.
sections.criteria: Desired-state control plane with a reconciler and an assignment service; tasks with externally stored positions so they can move; isolation designed by blast radius (per-tenant worker groups or process-level isolation for risky plugins, resource limits) with its cost stated; restarts with exponential backoff, a failure budget and a terminal failed state that is shown to the customer; incremental, membership-change-tolerant assignment so unrelated tasks keep running; progress-based health (records and positions advancing) as well as liveness; staged plugin rollout with canaries and fast rollback; secrets redacted from every error path; status latency within {{status_seconds}} seconds; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are plugins written by the service?
clarifications.a: Most are; some are from partners. Assume any of them can leak memory, hang or crash.

clarifications.q: Can a task be moved between workers safely?
clarifications.a: Yes, if its positions are stored outside the worker; a move costs a restart.

clarifications.q: Do customers choose task counts?
clarifications.a: They choose a maximum; you may run fewer.

clarifications.q: What counts as failed?
clarifications.a: Your design should define it: crashed, stuck with no progress, or erroring on every record.

hints: Separate desired state (what should run) from observed state (what is running); a reconciler moves one toward the other.
Decide the unit of isolation (process, container, worker group per tenant) by cost and blast radius, and say what a noisy neighbour can still do.
"Running" is not "making progress". Status needs a progress signal, not only a liveness one.
followups: Walk through creating a connector with 8 tasks, from the API call to the first record written.
One tenant's source database goes down and its 400 tasks start crash-looping. What happens to the workers they share and to other tenants?
How do you roll out a new plugin version to {{tasks}} tasks, and how do you notice that it is worse before it reaches all of them?
How do you detect a task that reports running but has copied nothing for two hours?
How do you size and bin-pack workers, and when do you split a tenant onto dedicated workers?

rules.ask: One worker restarts every minute. How many unrelated tasks stop each time in your design, and how do you make that number small?
Is one task one container? What does that cost at {{tasks}} tasks, and what do you lose if many tasks share one?
After how many restarts do you stop, what state do you show, and who is told?
What does dedicating workers per tenant cost at {{tenants}} tenants, and which tenants actually need it?
Which metric tells you the canary is worse, and how long do you wait before widening?

incidents: One tenant's source database is down. Its 400 tasks crash and restart every few seconds; each restart changes worker group membership and pauses tasks of about 200 other tenants on the same workers.
A new version of a popular sink plugin leaks memory. Workers run out of memory after about six hours, and the tasks they held move together to other workers, which then run out of memory too.
A customer's sink connector shows running for two hours while it has written nothing; it is blocked on a lock in the destination database, and the customer finds out from their own users.
A task's error message, shown in the console and sent to logs, contains the full connection string with a password.

templates.title: Partition reassignment planner: evening out broker load under replication throttles
templates.subtopic: replica placement, throttled data movement, leader balance

sections.scenario: A Kafka cluster of {{brokers}} brokers holds {{partitions}} partition replicas across three racks. Load has drifted: a few brokers carry far more disk, network and leader traffic than others, and {{new_brokers}} new, empty brokers have just been added. Moving a replica means copying its whole log to the new broker, which competes with producers and consumers for disk and network, so movement is limited by a replication throttle of about {{throttle_mb}} MB/s per broker.
sections.problem: Design a planner and executor that move replicas and leaders to even out load. Cover the inputs (per-partition size, bytes in and out, leader and follower placement, racks, broker capacity); the objective and hard constraints (rack-aware placement, disk headroom, keeping each partition's in-sync replicas at or above its minimum); how a plan is broken into batches and executed under the throttle; how progress is monitored and a plan paused or aborted; when leaders are moved instead of data; and how you estimate how long the plan takes before you start.
sections.constraints: Producer p99 latency must not rise by more than 20% during movement. A partition must never have fewer in-sync replicas than its minimum because of the plan. The plan must survive a broker failure mid-run. Operators must be able to say how much data is left to move and when it will finish.
sections.assumptions: All sizes and rates are hypothetical. For this exercise, a reassignment adds the new replicas first, lets them copy and catch up, and removes the old replicas only once the new ones are in sync, so a partition's replica set is temporarily larger; leaders can be moved among in-sync replicas without copying data. This exercise's model; check current docs.
sections.criteria: Inputs and capacity model per broker (disk, network in and out, leaders) and per partition; an objective that trades load evenness against bytes moved, with rack-aware and minimum-in-sync hard constraints; a duration estimate from bytes, throttle and concurrency, plus the catch-up condition (copy rate above the partition's incoming rate); small batches with a concurrency budget per broker, monitoring of in-sync state, latency and progress, and safe pause, resume and abort; leader moves as a separate, cheap step applied gradually; recovery from a broker failure mid-plan; continuous balancing with hysteresis so it does not flap; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do all partitions need moving?
clarifications.a: No. Choose what to move; moving less data for most of the benefit is better.

clarifications.q: Is the throttle per broker or per partition?
clarifications.a: Per broker, inbound and outbound, as stated.

clarifications.q: Can I move leaders only?
clarifications.a: Yes; it is cheap, but it balances only leader traffic, not disk.

clarifications.q: What does producer latency depend on here?
clarifications.a: Producers wait for all in-sync replicas to acknowledge; slow followers on busy brokers raise it.

hints: Score a plan by load evenness gained per byte moved; moving a huge, quiet partition is rarely worth it.
A new replica can only join the in-sync set if it copies faster than the partition receives new data. Check that against the throttle.
Execute in small batches with a budget of concurrent moves per broker, so a failure or an abort leaves little half done.
followups: Estimate the duration of a plan that moves 14 TB onto {{new_brokers}} new brokers at {{throttle_mb}} MB/s each. What makes the real run slower than the estimate?
One partition receives data faster than its share of the throttle. What happens to its new replica, and what do you do?
A broker fails halfway through a batch. What state are the affected partitions in, and how does the executor resume?
How do you choose between moving data and moving only leaders for a broker that is hot on network but not on disk?
How would you run this continuously, as a background balancer, without it fighting operators or flapping?

rules.ask: Your greedy step picks the most loaded broker's biggest partition. Show a case where that moves far more data than needed.
Raise the throttle to finish faster. Which brokers' producers feel it first, and how do you know before they complain?
How do you choose the batch size, and does it change as the plan runs?
Moving leaders to the new brokers shifts consumer fetch traffic too. What happens to their network?
At {{partitions}} replicas, how long does your solver take, and what do you do when the cluster changes while it runs?

incidents: A plan that moves 14 TB onto the {{new_brokers}} new brokers at {{throttle_mb}} MB/s each has run for twice its estimated time and is 40% done: three hot partitions receive data faster than their throttled copy rate, so their new replicas never join the in-sync set, and their old replicas cannot be removed.

A source broker fails mid-batch. For several partitions the replica set now contains the half-copied new replica and one surviving old one; with a minimum of two in-sync replicas, producers to those partitions start receiving not-enough-replicas errors.
Leaders are moved to the {{new_brokers}} new brokers in one step. Consumers follow the leaders, and one new broker's outbound network saturates within minutes.

The throttle was raised from {{throttle_mb}} MB/s to three times that to finish overnight. Producer p99 on two old brokers rises fourfold, because their disks are serving both the copies and consumers reading old data.

templates.title: Changing an unsafe default that some customers rely on
templates.subtopic: safe defaults, customer impact, staged change

default: producers are acknowledged once only the partition leader has written a record
a replica that is not in sync may become leader when no in-sync replica is available
topics are created automatically, with default settings, the first time any client names one

sections.scenario: You lead the team that owns the defaults of a managed streaming service. In this exercise's service, by default {{default}}. Over the last year, {{incidents}} customer incidents involving lost or misplaced data were traced to that default. Changing it is safer for almost everyone, but telemetry suggests about {{share}} of active workloads rely on the current behaviour, some deliberately (for lower latency, for availability, or because their tooling expects it) and some without knowing.
sections.problem: How do you change the default? Cover how you establish who depends on the current behaviour and why; whether the change applies to new resources only or to existing ones too; how customers are told, and how far ahead; what opt-out exists and for how long; how you stage the rollout and what you watch; how you handle a large customer who objects; and how you decide, and who decides, if the evidence is mixed. Then tell me about a real time you changed a behaviour that others relied on, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The service promises not to break existing workloads without notice. Some affected customers are large and vocal; others have no active contact. You cannot see what customers' applications do with the data, only how their clients behave.
sections.assumptions: The service, the figures and the incident count are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts from evidence (the incidents, telemetry on who relies on the behaviour, separating deliberate from inherited use, talking to a sample of each); chooses a staged change (new resources first, an explicit setting that keeps the old behaviour for those who want it, notice periods, a time-boxed opt-out, then existing resources only where it is safe or with consent); defines stop criteria and monitoring before rolling out; handles the objecting customer with options, not a fight; names decision owners and escalates with a fair summary when evidence is mixed; measures the result (incidents before and after); real example with personal contribution and what was learned, or an honest "have not" with sound reasoning.

clarifications.q: Do the incidents have anything in common?
clarifications.a: In most, the customer did not know the default existed until they lost or misplaced data.

clarifications.q: Who can approve a change to a default?
clarifications.a: Your team proposes; product management and the support organisation must agree; a director decides if they do not.

clarifications.q: Is there a deadline?
clarifications.a: No external one. A competitor's comparison of safe defaults is circulating, which raises the pressure.

clarifications.q: Can customers set the old behaviour explicitly?
clarifications.a: Yes; an explicit setting is never changed, only the default.

hints: Split the workloads that rely on the behaviour into those that chose it and those that inherited it; they need different treatment.
"New resources first" is a common way to change a default without breaking anything that already runs.
Decide in advance what signal would make you stop the rollout.
followups: How exactly would you find the workloads that rely on the current behaviour, and how confident can you be in that list?
A large customer says the change will cost them latency they have contracts around. What do you do?
Do you change existing resources at all? If so, how, and on what timeline?
Two weeks into the rollout, support tickets rise. How do you decide whether to pause, and who decides?
In your real example, what did you get wrong about who depended on the old behaviour?

rules.ask: Customers with no active contact never read the notice. How do you reach them, and what happens to them on the day?
How long does the opt-out live? What stops it from becoming the new permanent default for a third of your customers?
Two years later, half the fleet still runs the old default. Is that acceptable? What would you do next?
Telemetry shows clients' behaviour, not intent. How do you tell a deliberate choice from an inherited one?
What did you personally propose, and what did you change your mind about?

templates.title: A fleet-wide major-version upgrade every team keeps postponing
templates.subtopic: upgrades, deadlines, incentives, tooling

blocker: the removal of a client protocol version that about 15% of applications still use
a change to a consumer default that some consumer groups depend on
a metadata migration that needs every cluster restarted in a fixed order

sections.scenario: Your platform team runs {{clusters}} streaming clusters used by many product teams. The major version they run stops receiving security fixes in {{months}} months. The new major version needs work from application teams because of {{blocker}}. The upgrade has been on the roadmap and postponed {{postponed}} quarters in a row; each team has a good local reason, and most of the work to unblock it sits with them, not with you.
sections.problem: How do you get the fleet upgraded before support ends? Cover how you size the real work per team; what you can take off their plate with tooling or compatibility measures; how you set and communicate a deadline that people believe; how you track progress and deal with the last few teams; what you do if a team says it cannot do it in time; and how you keep the next major upgrade from turning out the same way. Then tell me about a real time you drove a change that others had to do the work for, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You have no authority over the application teams' roadmaps. Running unsupported software past the deadline is not acceptable for the security team. Your own team has three engineers available for this.
sections.assumptions: The figures and the version details are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Measures the real impact first (client versions from broker telemetry, a scan of configurations and code, a short survey) and sizes work per team; reduces the work on the platform side (compatibility measures with an end date, automated detection, upgrade guides, pull requests opened for teams); sets a credible deadline backed by leadership with an agreed exception process; tracks progress visibly and works the long tail one team at a time; handles the team with a launch with options rather than threats; changes the process so future upgrades are routine (supported-version policy, continuous compatibility checks, small regular upgrades); real example with personal contribution and measurable outcome, or an honest "have not" with sound reasoning.

clarifications.q: Do teams know about the deadline?
clarifications.a: It has been announced twice in a newsletter.

clarifications.q: Is there leadership support?
clarifications.a: Your director supports it but has not asked the other directors for anything yet.

clarifications.q: Can the platform keep both versions running for a while?
clarifications.a: Some compatibility is possible at a cost, and it does not remove the deadline.

clarifications.q: How much work is it per team?
clarifications.a: Unknown; estimates range from a day to several weeks.

hints: Find out where the work actually is before asking anyone for time; most fleets have a long tail of easy cases and a few hard ones.
Every change you make on the platform side, such as compatibility shims, automated checks or code changes you open yourselves, removes a reason to postpone.
A deadline people believe needs an owner above the teams and a visible consequence, agreed in advance.
followups: How would you find out, within two weeks, which applications are actually affected and how much work each has?
What would you build or change on the platform side so that most teams need almost nothing from their own roadmap?
One month before the deadline, five teams have not started, including one with a key launch. What do you do?
How do you prevent the next major upgrade from repeating this?
In your real example, what finally made people move, and was it what you expected?

rules.ask: What exactly does the escalation ask the other directors for, and what happens to a team that still does not upgrade?
Whose numbers are on it, and how do you keep it from becoming a shaming board that teams resent?
How long does the shim live, and what stops it from becoming the reason the next upgrade is postponed too?
Which part did you personally do or decide, and what did you hand to others?
Who grants an exception, on what evidence, and what does the team owe in return?

templates.title: A strategic customer asks for a custom feature that would fork the product
templates.subtopic: customer pressure, forks, open-source upstream

feature: a time-to-live on each record, enforced by the broker, which the open-source project does not support
a broker-side partitioner that routes by a field inside the record value
a way for their clients to skip schema checks on one high-volume topic

sections.scenario: You are the technical lead for the core streaming engine of a managed service built on an open-source project. A strategic customer, worth about {{revenue}} of the business's revenue in their region, asks for {{feature}} within {{weeks}} weeks, and says they will move to a competitor otherwise. Your sales team has half-promised it. Building it in your version of the engine only would make that version diverge from the open-source project, which every future upgrade would then have to carry.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you find out what problem the customer is trying to solve; what options you lay out (including ways to solve their problem without the feature as asked); how you weigh the customer against the long-term cost of a divergent engine; who makes the decision and how you bring them the trade-off; how you work with sales and the customer; and, if you build something, how you keep it from becoming a permanent fork. Then tell me about a real time you said no, or "not like that", to an important customer or stakeholder, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The {{weeks}} weeks are the customer's stated deadline. Your team is fully booked. Anything added to the engine must be supported for every customer who turns it on.
sections.assumptions: The customer, the revenue share and the deadline are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Goes to the underlying need with the customer's engineers before deciding; lays out options with honest costs, including solving the problem outside the engine and an upstream path; prices divergence over future releases; brings the trade-off to the right decider with a clear recommendation and respects the decision; works with sales to reset expectations without blame; if building, keeps it behind a clean interface, aimed at upstream, with an exit plan; real example with personal contribution and the outcome for the relationship, or an honest "have not" with sound reasoning.

clarifications.q: Has anyone asked the customer why they need it?
clarifications.a: Only sales, and the answer was "they need it for compliance".

clarifications.q: Does the open-source community want something similar?
clarifications.a: There is an old proposal for something close that stalled for lack of a contributor.

clarifications.q: Who decides?
clarifications.a: The product lead for the engine, with your recommendation; the business owner of the account has a strong voice.

clarifications.q: Can the customer's problem be solved outside the engine?
clarifications.a: Possibly, in the client, in a stream processing job or with existing configuration; that is for you to find out.

hints: Ask what outcome the customer needs; a request for a feature is often one possible solution to a problem with several.
Put a cost on divergence in upgrade effort per release, not only on building the feature.
Contributing upstream is slower but keeps one engine; say what it would take to get there in time, or what a bridge would look like.
followups: What questions would you ask the customer's engineers in the first meeting?
Lay out three options with cost, time and risk for each, including one that does not change the engine.
The account owner says, "just build it, we will clean it up later". How do you respond?
If you do build it, how do you keep it from turning into a permanent fork?
In your real example, what happened to the relationship with the customer or stakeholder afterwards?

rules.ask: Upstream review could take longer than {{weeks}} weeks. What do you ship in the meantime, and what happens if upstream accepts a different design?
The customer leaves. Who carries that decision, and how did you make sure they were deciding with the full picture?
Who supports that path when it breaks for the customer at 3 a.m., and is that cheaper than the feature?
Six months on, two more customers turn the flag on. Is it still a customer-specific feature?
Sales half-promised it already. How do you reset the expectation without making sales look bad to the customer?

templates.title: Leading one team across three time zones with handoffs instead of meetings
templates.subtopic: distributed teams, written handoffs, on-call, decision making

sections.scenario: You lead a team of {{size}} engineers who own {{owns}} for a managed streaming service. The team is split across the Americas, Europe and South Asia; working time shared by all three regions: {{overlap}}. Last month a customer-facing incident passed through {{handoffs}} handoffs before it was resolved, and each handoff lost time while the next person rebuilt context. Design reviews wait a week for a meeting everyone can attend, and engineers in one region say decisions are made while they sleep.
sections.problem: How do you make the team work well across the three time zones? Cover how work and ownership are divided between regions; what a good handoff contains and how it is made, for incidents and for ordinary work; how decisions are made in writing and when a meeting is still needed; how on-call is organised; how you notice and fix it when one region feels second-class; and how you would measure whether things are better in three months. Then tell me about a real time you led or worked in a distributed team and changed how it worked, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Moving people or hiring in one place is not an option this year. Customer incidents must be worked around the clock. No one should routinely work outside their own hours.
sections.assumptions: The team, regions and incident are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses where time is lost (the incident timeline, decision latency, who waits for whom) before changing anything; gives each region ownership of whole areas, including decisions and design; a written handoff format used for incidents and ordinary work, with an explicit owner at every moment; written decisions with comment windows and a few meetings with fairly shared times; on-call designed so incidents are followed around the clock without hero hours; develops seniority in every region; measures the change (time lost per handoff, decision latency, survey of each region); real example with personal contribution and honest outcomes, or an honest "have not" with sound reasoning.

clarifications.q: Are the regions equal in size and seniority?
clarifications.a: No. Most senior engineers are in one region.

clarifications.q: Is there an incident tool?
clarifications.a: Yes, with a timeline; people rarely write in it during an incident.

clarifications.q: How are design decisions recorded today?
clarifications.a: In meetings and chat threads; there is no single place.

clarifications.q: Are you in one of the regions?
clarifications.a: Yes, in the one with most senior engineers.

hints: A handoff is a written artefact: state, hypotheses ruled in and out, next steps, and who owns it now.
Give each region ownership of whole things, not leftovers from another region's day.
Written decisions with a stated comment window let everyone take part without a meeting.
followups: What would a good incident handoff note look like for last month's incident?
How would you divide ownership so that each region owns whole pieces of work, including design and decisions?
How do you make sure the region without senior engineers grows and is not just the night shift?
Three months on, how do you know whether it worked?
In your real example, what did you change, and what still did not work?

rules.ask: Follow-the-sun means every incident crosses at least one handoff. When would you rather keep one person on it longer?
Which meetings survive your change, at what time, and which region pays the inconvenience?
How long do people get to comment, and what happens to a decision that someone in another region disagrees with after it is made?
What did you personally change, and how did you find out it was working?
Rotating meeting times shares the pain. How does it affect the people with caring responsibilities in each region?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for event streams with ordering and replay guarantees
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, ordering and replay

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
guarantee: per-key ordering, even when producers retry and partitions are added
replaying 90 days of history into a new consumer without disturbing live ones
results that count every event exactly once when consumers crash mid-batch
old events that must stay readable after the schema changes many times

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if its inputs arrived as event streams of {{events}} of events per second, and its users required {{guarantee}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if the system were built on event streams with {{guarantee}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The event-stream setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible event-stream analysis that starts from keys and ordering, names assumptions of once-only and in-order delivery, and addresses {{guarantee}} incrementally (for example keyed partitioning with stable partition counts, idempotent producers and consumers, transactional or idempotent outputs, separate replay paths with quotas, schema compatibility rules enforced at write time); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a streaming system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the event-stream part is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, ordering, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the event-stream question, start from the key: what must be ordered relative to what, and what may be processed independently.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design assume data arrives once and in order? What breaks first with event streams?
How would you provide {{guarantee}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?
